questions.question: Which description correctly separates an Iceberg table format from its surrounding systems?
options: Iceberg is the query engine that executes every scan
Iceberg defines versioned table metadata; file formats store contents, and a catalog locates current metadata
Iceberg is an object store that replaces Parquet
Iceberg is only a directory-naming convention for partitions
questions.explanation: Iceberg defines how schemas, partition specs, snapshots, manifests, and files form a table. Compute engines execute work, file formats encode file contents, and catalogs provide the current metadata location.

questions.question: A reader pins snapshot 4401 while another writer commits snapshot 4402. What should the pinned reader observe?
options: A mixture of files from both snapshots
Snapshot 4402 as soon as any new data file appears in storage
The complete file set referenced by snapshot 4401 until the reader refreshes or chooses another snapshot
No rows because readers must lock the catalog during a commit
questions.explanation: Readers resolve one committed snapshot. Atomic metadata replacement lets existing readers remain on the old snapshot while refreshed readers can resolve the new current snapshot.

questions.question: A table evolves from day(event_time) to hour(event_time) plus identity(region). What happens to existing daily files?
options: The metadata change immediately rewrites every old file
The old files remain under their original partition spec, while new files use the new default spec
The old files become invisible to queries
Queries must switch from event_time to physical partition-directory columns
questions.explanation: Partition evolution changes future writer behavior. Existing files remain in manifests tied to their original spec, and readers project source-column predicates through every represented spec.

questions.question: Why does Iceberg use both a manifest list and manifest files during scan planning?
options: The manifest list can prune whole manifests before manifests are opened; manifests then prune individual files
The manifest list stores every table row, while manifests store SQL text
Both files are identical backups and must always be scanned fully
Manifest files are only needed when a query has no predicate
questions.explanation: The manifest list summarizes manifests, including partition ranges. Candidate manifests then expose file-level partition tuples and statistics for a second pruning stage.

questions.question: Two append writers plan from the same base snapshot. The first commits successfully, so the second loses the metadata-pointer race. What is the appropriate next step for the second append?
options: Make its data visible by moving files into the first writer's directory
Overwrite the current metadata pointer without checking the new state
Refresh current metadata, validate its assumptions, reapply the append, and retry while reusing safe immutable artifacts
Delete the first writer's snapshot
questions.explanation: A lost optimistic race is not permission to overwrite current state. Appends can commonly rebase onto refreshed metadata and reuse their prepared data and manifest files when validation succeeds.

questions.question: A compaction prepared file AB to replace source files A and B. Before it commits, another writer replaces B with B2. What must the compaction do after refreshing?
options: Commit AB anyway because compaction never changes logical rows
Restore B so the original plan becomes valid
Validate only that A still exists
Stop and replan because one required source file is no longer in the current snapshot
questions.explanation: A rewrite can retry only if all files it intends to replace are still present. Since B disappeared, the stale compaction output cannot safely replace the refreshed table state.
